title: The Aorta Is One Organ; Our Response Is Not: A Global Case for Systems Redesign in Aortic Syndromes
content: The aorta is a single arterial organ, yet the clinical response to its diseases is fragmented across specialties, institutions, and nations. Acute aortic syndromes remain lethal at every stage of the care continuum: a large share of patients with type A dissection die before reaching any hospital, roughly half before reaching a specialist centre, a substantial proportion are misdiagnosed at first medical contact, and untreated mortality accrues at approximately one to two percent per hour. Crucially, the same disease produces markedly different outcomes across health systems. Operative mortality at 30 days ranges from 7.6% in the Japan Cardiovascular Surgery Database to 16.9% in the German GERAADA registry, and this international variation is itself the strongest available evidence that outcomes are determined by system design rather than by biology alone. This review synthesises registry, population, and health-services data from Europe, Japan, North America, and low- and middle-income settings to characterise where the pathway fails and what each system has already demonstrated. We argue that the next material advance in aortic care will come not from a single device, scan, or guideline but from architecture, and we propose a five-pillar framework (Prevention, Presentation, Pathway, Person, and Learning) mapped throughout to published exemplars and to future-research priorities.
